settings.content: Chapter six of The Ring and Jewellery Care Guide

settings.heading: Stones Are Rarely Lost Without Notice
settings.body:
Stones are almost never lost without warning. They are lost because the warning was missed, or because it was worn through before anyone looked.

A claw thins gradually. A bezel edge lifts after a knock. A pavé bead wears until it no longer holds its stone. Every one of those changes can be seen or felt weeks before a stone goes. This chapter is about learning to notice them.

Chains, clasps and earring fittings fail in their own way, and they have their own section further down.

settings.cells: Claw or prong | The tip thins with abrasion until it no longer holds the stone | Claws that catch on knitwear, feel sharp, or look flattened or shortened
Rub-over or bezel | The metal edge lifts or thins after impact | A visible gap at the rim, or a stone that has shifted within it
Pavé and micro-pavé | Individual beads wear, or a bead is knocked off | A dark or dull spot in a line of stones, or a stone sitting lower than its neighbours
Channel | The channel wall spreads after impact and releases stones | Movement in the line, or a wall that no longer looks parallel
Tension and open settings | Distortion of the band changes the grip on the stone | Any change in the ring's roundness at all

settings.heading: How Each One Fails
settings.intro: Find your setting in the first column, then learn the third. That is the one you are looking for at home.
settings.headers: Setting | How it fails | What to watch

settings.heading: The fabric test
settings.body: Pass the ring gently over fine knitwear or a microfibre cloth. A claw that has begun to lift will snag before it is visible to the eye. This is the single most reliable home check for claw wear.

settings.heading: The thirty-second evening check
settings.body: Under good light: is the centre stone still sitting level? Is any claw visibly raised or displaced? Does a soft cloth catch on anything that it did not before? Is the band still circular?

settings.heading: Every few weeks is enough
settings.body: Once a fortnight suits a ring in daily wear. The point is to notice a change, which only works if you have looked recently enough to remember how it looked.

settings.heading: Handle the ring by its band
settings.body: Picking a ring up by the band rather than pressing over the centre stone keeps fingerprints off and avoids repeated pressure on fine claws and delicate settings.

settings.heading: Thirty Seconds, and a Piece of Knitwear
settings.intro: Neither of these replaces a workshop inspection. Both catch sudden damage early, which is when it is cheapest to fix.

settings.heading: Stop Wearing It, and Stop Testing It
settings.body:
Do not keep testing a loose stone. Every movement enlarges the seat inside the setting and turns a small repair into a lost stone.

Put the ring in its box and contact us the same day. A claw retip is a small, inexpensive job. Sourcing a matching replacement stone is neither.

settings.label: A stone that moves, clicks or rattles
settings.note: Stop wearing the ring and contact us the same day.

settings.label: A claw that repeatedly catches, or feels sharp
settings.note: Catching on knitwear usually means a claw has lifted or worn thin.

settings.label: A visible gap around a gemstone
settings.note: Most common on a rub-over setting after an impact.

settings.label: A bent, uneven or distorted setting
settings.note: Pressure has moved metal that is holding a stone in place.

settings.label: A band that is no longer circular
settings.note: A change in shape transfers pressure through the setting and loosens stones.

settings.label: A crack, deep dent or sudden change after an impact
settings.note: Have it looked at straight away, whenever the last inspection was.

settings.label: An unexpected and persistent change in fit
settings.note: Worth a conversation before it becomes a resize.

settings.heading: Seven Signs Worth a Message
settings.intro: Fine scratches, a polish softening and platinum taking on a patina are all normal. These are not.

settings.cells: Daily wear, pavé or claw-set | Annually
Daily wear, plain or rub-over set | Annually, or every two years
Chains and pendants worn daily | Annually, checking the bail and the link beneath it
After any significant impact | Immediately, regardless of the last check

settings.heading: When Settings Should Be Checked
settings.intro: The annual condition inspection and standard professional clean are complimentary for the life of every piece we supply.
settings.note: Do not wait for the annual date if a stone moves, a claw catches, the ring changes shape or it takes a significant impact. Contact us the same week.

settings.heading: A Pendant Is Lost at the Fitting
settings.body:
A pendant is rarely lost because the chain broke in the middle. It is lost at a fitting: the bail, a jump ring, or the clasp. Almost always after weeks of small warnings that were easy to miss.

Fittings are the parts that move, and anything that moves against metal wears. The useful news is that a worn clasp or a thinning bail is a straightforward workshop job, provided it is caught while it is still a repair.

settings.cells: Chain links | Links thin where they rub, particularly at the back of the neck and either side of the clasp | Kinking, a section that hangs differently, or a link stretched into an oval
Bail | Constant movement wears both the bail and the link running through it | A bail worn thin underneath, or a pendant that has begun to tilt forward
Clasps | The spring tires, or the catch wears until it no longer closes fully | A clasp that opens under light pressure, feels slack, or needs a second attempt to close
Jump rings | Soldered rings open under load, and unsoldered rings simply pull apart | A visible gap, or an end that no longer sits flush against its neighbour
Posts and butterflies | Posts bend and thin at the base, and butterfly backs lose their grip | A post that flexes easily, or a back that slides off without resistance

settings.heading: How Fittings Wear
settings.headers: Fitting | How it fails | What to watch

settings.heading: How to do it
settings.body: Hold the chain either side of the clasp and pull gently, firmly enough to feel resistance but not hard enough to strain it. Do the same either side of the bail, and flex an earring post lightly between finger and thumb.

settings.heading: What a failure looks like
settings.body: Anything that gives, clicks or opens has been telling you so for some time. Stop wearing the piece and contact us the same week.

settings.heading: Repair it before it fails
settings.body: A worn clasp or a thinning bail is a straightforward workshop job. A pendant lost in the street is not recoverable at any price.

settings.heading: Storing chains
settings.body: Chains tangle and kink when they are stored loose, and a kinked link is a weak link. Fasten the clasp before putting a chain away, then lay it flat or hang it rather than dropping it into a dish.

settings.heading: Keep chains away from rings
settings.body: A claw setting will always find a chain in a shared box. Use individual compartments or soft pouches so that settings and stones cannot rub against one another.

settings.heading: Once a Month, and Store Them Properly
settings.intro: The fittings equivalent of the fabric test. It takes less than a minute for a whole jewellery box.

settings.q: How often should my ring be inspected?
settings.a: Annually for anything worn daily, and every two years for occasional wear. Immediately after any significant impact, whenever the last check was. The condition inspection and standard professional clean are complimentary for the life of the piece.

settings.q: What exactly is the fabric test?
settings.a: Pass the ring gently over fine knitwear or a microfibre cloth. A claw that has started to lift will snag before you can see it. It is the most reliable home check for claw wear, and it takes seconds.

settings.q: A claw has started catching. What should I do?
settings.a: Stop wearing the ring and contact us. A new catch usually means movement, damage or worn metal, and a claw retip is small and inexpensive compared with replacing a stone.

settings.q: I can hear a rattle in my ring.
settings.a: Stop testing it. Every movement enlarges the seat inside the setting. Put the ring in its box and contact us the same day.

settings.q: My band looks oval rather than round.
settings.a: It has been compressed or distorted. Stop wearing it, because a change in shape transfers pressure through the setting and loosens stones. Do not try to bend it back either: metal work-hardens, and a second bend is where it cracks.

settings.q: Is a rub-over setting safer than claws?
settings.a: They fail differently rather than one being universally safer. A claw thins at the tip until it no longer holds the stone, while a rub-over edge lifts or thins after an impact and leaves a visible gap at the rim.
Fasten the clasp first, then lay the chain flat or hang it rather than dropping it into a dish, and keep chains apart from rings. Chains kink when stored loose, and a kinked link is a weak link.

settings.q: A stone has fallen out. What happens now?
settings.a: Stop wearing the ring and do not test the setting any further. Search carefully before moving around: clothing turn-ups, pockets, the sink trap if it happened near water, and the floor along your route. Put the ring, and the stone if you find it, into a box, then send us photographs of the setting. We will tell you whether it is a repair, a reset or an insurance matter, and what it is likely to cost, before you send anything.
